evidence.claim: The acceptance mechanism for candidates in Meta Harness Phase 2 is fundamentally contradicted: a candidate that performed worse (score decreased from 68.2% to 59.1%) was kept, violating the stated rule to reject worse candidates.
evidence.excerpt: Keeping a worse candidate fundamentally contradicts the method's described acceptance mechanism.

judge_panel.reason: The paper explicitly explains that in Meta Harness Phase 2, 'Every candidate generated during Meta Harness's second optimization round performed worse than the existing agent, and its score fell to 59.1%.' The paper clarifies that the kept file (output_noise_compaction.py) was 'the candidate that was ultimately kept' but also notes 'the released artifacts do not include the rejected candidates from that round.' The 59.1% is not the score of a worse candidate that was wrongly accepted — it is the best available candidate that was still worse than the transfer score. The method rejects candidates worse than the current best, but all generated candidates were worse, so the best-available was kept, which is consistent with the method's acceptance mechanism.

The paper says Meta Harness candidates are "accepted or rejected based on evaluation feedback on the current task set" (Sec. 4.3), but Appendix C then states: "Every candidate generated during Meta Harness’s second optimization round scored worse than its Phase-1-optimized agent... The one Phase 2 harness file released here ... is the candidate that was ultimately kept." That is an unresolved internal contradiction.

The paper states that Meta Harness candidates "are accepted or rejected based on evaluation feedback" (Section 4.3), but later reports that "Every candidate generated during Meta Harness's second optimization round scored worse... The one Phase 2 harness file released here... is the candidate that was ultimately kept" (Appendix C). The paper does not explain why a strictly worse candidate was kept instead of being rejected to preserve the Phase 1 agent's score.
